opening.headline: When the serving endpoint is slow or intermittently fails, it explains where to look for the root cause—among setup, capacity, or model.
body: At the serving endpoint, there are instances where response latency spikes and some requests fail during specific time periods. Even if the symptoms are the same, the root cause can lead to completely different solutions—some requiring configuration changes, others requiring increased capacity, and others requiring changes to the model itself.

In this class, we examine what Databricks Model Serving serves, what settings are defined when creating endpoints, the nature of route optimization and Foundation Model APIs, and finally follow a structured approach to categorizing latency causes into settings, capacity, and model.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the configuration of model serving endpoints and route optimization.
The endpoint issue can be distinguished as to whether it originates from configuration, capacity, or model.

screens.title: The serving endpoint is slow or intermittently fails.
screens.lead: Three symptoms you may encounter when operating an endpoint. Each symptom, when selected, reveals points to consider.

visual.alt: A graph showing response latency increasing at specific times, accompanied by failure request indicators.

items.prompt: Response latency spikes and some requests fail during specific time periods.
items.answer: It is likely related to a situation where requests overwhelm the system, occurring only during specific time periods. To narrow down the cause, you should record the time period, the number of concurrent requests, and the nature of the failures together.

items.prompt: It's unclear whether the issue is due to configuration, capacity, or the model itself.
items.answer: Endpoints have settings such as compute type, scale-out size, idle behavior, and routing, on which the model runs. If we don't break down where time is spent across different layers, we risk making incorrect fixes.

items.prompt: The same symptoms can have completely different solutions depending on the cause.
items.answer: If capacity is insufficient, you must increase the scaling-out size; if only the first request is slow, changing the idle state action will not help; if the model logic is slow, adjusting the endpoint configuration will be ineffective. Therefore, the order of diagnosis is important.

screens.outro: The question for this class is this: What are the components of endpoints, and how should we break down the problem?

screens.title: Preview: Causes of serving delay
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thoughts are displayed. Please think about the answer mentally before entering or submitting it.

items.prompt: Where do you find the causes of latency in model serving?
items.answer: Delay can occur across all segments from when the request arrives until a response is generated. Network paths, queues, compute resources, and model execution are all potential candidates.

items.prompt: Have you ever separated response time into network latency and model execution phases?
items.answer: Dividing them allows us to explain why a model may be fast in execution but still slow overall. The fixed overhead incurred by the path becomes more significant as the number of requests increases, so it must be examined separately alongside model execution time.

items.prompt: When simultaneous requests increase, what will reach its limit first?
items.answer: Often, the limit is reached when the number of concurrent requests that can be processed at once hits a threshold. If the concurrent processing capacity falls below the product of requests per second and model execution time, requests will queue up and experience significant delays.

screens.outro: First, let's confirm what Model Serving is serving.

screens.title: Model Serving and Models That Can Be Served
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn what Model Serving is and which models it can serve.

visual.alt: Diagram showing a model serving endpoint providing three types of models via a REST API.
labels: Serverless Computing: Automatic scaling and shrinking based on demand

tabs.label: What is Model Serving?
tabs.body:
Model Serving is an integrated interface that deploys, manages, and enables inference for AI and ML models across real-time and batch inference. Served models are provided via REST APIs, allowing connectivity to web or client applications.

By leveraging serverless computing, it automatically scales up or down to match demand, optimizing latency while minimizing costs. All models and endpoints can be managed from a single dashboard, with permissions, usage limits, and quality monitoring all handled in one place.

tabs.label: Custom Model
tabs.body:
Python model packaged in MLflow format. This model can be deployed for models registered in Unity Catalog or workspace model registry. Examples include scikit-learn, XGBoost, PyTorch, and Hugging Face transformer models.

Agent serving is also supported as a custom model. To create an endpoint, you need a model registered in the registry, permissions for the model, and workspace configuration.

tabs.label: Foundation models
tabs.body:
The foundation models hosted by Databricks are provided via Foundation Model APIs. The base models can be used immediately on a pay-per-token basis, while workloads requiring performance guarantees or fine-tuned models are deployed with provisioned throughput.

Models hosted outside of Databricks are accessed through external model capabilities. Endpoints serving these models can also be centrally managed within Databrisks, enabling management of multiple LLM providers from a single location.

tabs.label: Management functions
tabs.body: You can manage permissions for all endpoints, including those hosting models externally, set usage restrictions, and monitor quality on the serving interface. You cannot use the prefix `databricks-` for endpoint names. This prefix is reserved for endpoints pre-configured by Databricks.

screens.outro: Next, let's examine each setting defined when creating an endpoint.

screens.title: Endpoint Generation Settings
screens.lead: The following is an example of an endpoint creation request. Selecting the highlighted sections allows you to verify the meaning of each setting and the symptoms that occur when it is misaligned.

visual.alt: A screenshot showing the selection of service entity, compute, scaling out, scale to zero, and route optimization in the service endpoint creation screen.

marks.note: Refers to the serving model by the three-part name in Unity Catalog. Endpoint creation or renewal fails with permission errors if the name or permissions do not match.
The model version being served. You can add multiple models or versions as serving entities at a single endpoint and distribute traffic among them.

This is a compute instance type. It can use either a CPU or a GPU, and if using a GPU, you select from GPU workloads such as GPU_SMALL or GPU_MEDIUM. For models that require more memory, CPU_MEDIUM or CPU_LARGE instance types are available. Choosing a smaller instance type in terms of memory or GPU capacity may result in slower performance or failure.

This is the compute scale-out size. "Small" corresponds to 0–4 concurrent requests, "Medium" to 8–16, and "Large" to 16–64. This value should be approximately equal to the product of requests per second and model execution time, and if insufficient, delays will occur when requests surge.

Determine whether to set the compute capacity to 0 for idle instances. While turning it on reduces costs, turning it back up from 0 results in cold start delays, and when set to 0, capacity is not guaranteed, so it is not recommended for operational endpoints.
This indicates whether route optimization is enabled. It can only be set when creating an endpoint and cannot be modified for existing endpoints.

screens.outro: Route optimization and foundation model serving have different characteristics, so I will examine them separately.

screens.title: Route Optimization and Foundation Model APIs
screens.lead: Select the button to change state and alternatively compare Route Optimization with Foundation Model APIs.

visual.alt: Difference between general paths and route-optimized paths, as well as the three modes of Foundation Model APIs, illustrated in the figure.

states.label: Route optimization
states.body:
When route optimization is enabled, Model Serving improves the network path for inference requests. Clients and models communicate more quickly and directly, significantly reducing overhead latency, increasing throughput and requests per second within the same configuration, and providing more stable latency. This is recommended for endpoints requiring high QPS and throughput.

There are some conditions: route optimization can only be enabled when creating a new endpoint and cannot be applied to existing endpoints. The query URL must be different, and authentication is supported only with Databricks OAuth tokens; personal access tokens are not supported. This feature is available only for custom models and feature serving endpoints, and does not apply to Foundation Model APIs or external model endpoints.

states.label: Foundation Model APIs
states.body:
Foundation Model APIs enable querying of Foundation Models hosted by Databricks through endpoints, and come in three modes. Pay-per-token is the simplest way to begin using Foundation Models. Provisioned throughput is recommended for all operational workloads requiring high throughput, performance guarantees, fine-tuned models, or additional security requirements. AI Functions optimized models are recommended for batch inference. 

Provisioned throughput includes two options: on-demand, which has no commitment, and reserved capacity, which secures dedicated capacity for a specified period. Therefore, it is a common workflow to transition from a starter mode to provisioned throughput when capacity guarantees are needed in operations.

screens.outro: Now, let's examine a case where we categorize the causes of delay into setup, capacity, and model.

screens.title: Explanation: Distinguishing whether the delay is due to a configuration issue or a capacity issue
screens.lead: This is the process where the instructor identifies the delay symptoms on endpoints and categorizes the root cause by capacity and model. Select the right arrow to follow along.

visual.alt: A decision flowchart starting from delayed symptoms, branching out based on the questions asked.
labels: Is it only slow when there are simultaneous requests?
Scale-out size vs QPS × execution time
Is the first request after idle period slow?
Model logic: Not resolvable by configuration

steps.title: Step 1: First, distinguish the pattern of delay
steps.body: First, distinguish whether delay is always high, increases only during bursts of concurrent requests, or is slow only on the first request after a period of inactivity. The pattern directly reveals the layering of the root cause. Before changing settings, compare the delay graph with request volume on the same time axis.

steps.title: Step 2: If always true, check the execution time and compute type.
steps.body: Even when traffic is low, if there is significant latency, it indicates that the time to process a single request is long. Check whether the model execution time is long or whether the compute type is smaller than the model itself. The model might be running on a CPU type with insufficient memory or a model that requires a GPU might be running on a CPU.

steps.title: Step 3: Calculate the scale-out size only if it increases when scaled out.
steps.body: If concurrent requests surge, there's a high likelihood that the concurrent processing capacity is insufficient. The required capacity is approximately the product of the number of requests per second and the model execution time. For example, if there are 20 requests per second with an execution time of 0.5 seconds, approximately 10 requests must be handled simultaneously. Thus, Small (0 to 4) is insufficient, while Medium (8 to 16) is appropriate.

steps.title: Step 4: Cold start occurs if the first request after idle period is slow
steps.body: If scale to zero is enabled and the first request after idle state is slow, this indicates a cold start as the compute resource scales back up from zero. Capacity guarantees are not provided, so this is not recommended for production endpoints. Disabling scale to zero resolves this, representing a trade-off between cost and latency.

steps.title: Step 5: If the QPS is high but the path overhead is significant, consider route optimization.
steps.body: If high QPS and throughput are required but significant overhead delays occur due to routing, consider route optimization. Since existing endpoints cannot be modified, new endpoints must be created, and the request URLs along with OAuth authentication calls need to be updated.

steps.title: Step 6: If the model logic is the root cause, it cannot be resolved by configuration alone.
steps.body: If a request is slow despite checking the compute resources, scaling, and routing, the issue lies in the logic of the serving model itself. In such cases, changing the endpoint settings will not resolve the problem; instead, the preprocessing, postprocessing, and inference code of the model must be improved, a new version created, and the serving version updated.

screens.outro: Finally, I will summarize the lecture content.

screens.title: Key Takeaway: Serving issues are categorized into configuration, capacity, and model.
screens.lead: This course content is summarized into three aspects: composition, diagnosis, and selection.

paragraphs: **Composition**: An endpoint consists of serving entity (model and version), traffic ratio, compute type, scale-out size, and scale-to-zero setting. The scale-out size is approximately set to the product of requests per second and model execution time.

**Diagnosis**: Categorize the cause based on the delay pattern. If slow performance is always observed, investigate execution time and compute type; if slow performance occurs only during scaling out, consider scaling-out size; if slow performance happens only on the first request after idle periods, suspect cold starts. If the root cause is in the model logic, it cannot be resolved by configuration changes.

**Selection**: Scaling to zero reduces costs but incurs cold start overhead. Route optimization must be configured at deployment time and is only available with custom models and feature serving endpoints. Foundation Model APIs charge per token at startup, but operate on provisioned throughput during ongoing operations.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: After the idle time has expired, only the first request is slow, and subsequent requests are normal. What is the most likely cause?
options: The scale-out size is less than QPS × execution time.
Cold start delay caused by scale to zero being enabled
Route optimization is disabled, causing the network path to become longer.
The logic of the currently serving model itself is always slow.
checks.explain: Scaling to zero instead of reducing idle costs introduces cold start delays on the first request. For this reason, it is not recommended for operational endpoints.

wrong.0: If capacity is insufficient, continuous slowdown occurs when multiple requests are made simultaneously.
wrong.2: Path overhead affects not only the first request but all requests throughout.
wrong.3: If the model logic is the cause, it is always slow and not limited to the first request.

checks.incorrectFeedback: Unfortunately, this is not the correct answer.

glossary.def: Databricks' serving functionality that deploys a model to a REST API endpoint and enables inference requests.
This is a query target composed of serving entities, compute resources, and traffic ratios.
An option that improves the network path of requests, reducing overhead delay and increasing throughput.
A feature that queries foundation models hosted by Databricks as an endpoint.
This setting reduces the compute capacity to 0 for idle instances. When restarting, it causes a cold start delay.

misconceptions.myth: Delay is caused by a slow model.
misconceptions.fact: Insufficient scale-out capacity, cold starts, and path overhead are causes of delays. You should analyze the patterns and divide the layers to verify.

misconceptions.myth: Route optimization can be enabled later.
misconceptions.fact: This can only be enabled when creating an endpoint, and existing endpoints cannot be modified.

misconceptions.myth: Scaling to zero is safe during operations.
misconceptions.fact: When 0, capacity is not guaranteed and a cold start delay may occur, which is not recommended for operational endpoints.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: Serving issues are categorized by configuration, capacity, and model.
The scaling-out size can be estimated as QPS × execution time.
Scaling to zero causes a cold start.
Route optimization is determined at the time of generation.
